name: Non-syndromic Diaphragmatic or Abdominal Wall Malformation

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and Imaging Diagnostic Criteria for Non-syndromic Diaphragmatic or Abdominal Wall Malformation

criteria.description: Presence of a congenital defect in the diaphragm confirmed by imaging or surgery
Identification of an abdominal wall malformation such as omphalocele or gastroschisis without associated syndromic features
No clinical or genetic evidence of syndromic association or chromosomal abnormalities
Prenatal ultrasound or MRI demonstrating diaphragmatic or abdominal wall defect
Respiratory distress in the neonatal period consistent with diaphragmatic hernia

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of a congenital diaphragmatic or abdominal wall defect confirmed by imaging or surgery, with absence of syndromic features
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis relies heavily on imaging and exclusion of syndromic causes.

pathognomonic.notes: Typically identified prenatally or at birth

pathognomonic.symptomName: Abdominal wall defect with herniation of abdominal contents
searchTerms: abdominal wall opening with organ protrusion

pathognomonic.symptomName: Neonatal respiratory distress due to pulmonary hypoplasia
pathognomonic.notes: Secondary to lung compression from herniated viscera
searchTerms: newborn breathing difficulty from small lungs
respiratory distress due to lung underdevelopment
pulmonary hypoplasia causing neonatal breathing problems

common.notes: Underdeveloped lungs due to space-occupying defect
Due to abdominal wall defects or associated anomalies
searchTerms: poor sucking or swallowing in neonates

common.notes: Rapid breathing secondary to compromised lung function
Sunken abdominal wall due to herniation
Low blood oxygen levels from impaired lung function

occasional.notes: Secondary to lung hypoplasia and vascular remodeling
Common in infants with diaphragmatic defects
Due to feeding difficulties and respiratory compromise
Due to displacement of thoracic structures
Signs of increased work of breathing

rare.notes: Rare and usually secondary to hypoxia
In cases of abdominal wall defects with rupture
searchTerms: infection due to open abdominal defect

laboratory: Arterial blood gas showing hypoxemia and respiratory acidosis
Normal metabolic panels unless secondary complications
imaging: Prenatal ultrasound or fetal MRI showing diaphragmatic or abdominal wall defect
Chest X-ray demonstrating herniation of abdominal contents into thoracic cavity
Echocardiography to assess pulmonary hypertension and cardiac anomalies
genetic: No consistent pathogenic variants identified in non-syndromic cases
Genetic testing to exclude syndromic or chromosomal abnormalities
other: Surgical findings confirming defect location and extent
Pulmonary function tests postnatally showing restrictive lung disease

distinguishingFeatures: Presence of additional syndromic features or genetic abnormalities
Multiple congenital anomalies beyond diaphragm or abdominal wall
Lung cysts or masses without herniation of abdominal contents
Elevated but intact diaphragm without true defect

redFlags: Severe neonatal respiratory distress unresponsive to ventilation
Visible abdominal wall defect with exposed viscera
Signs of pulmonary hypertension or cardiac compromise
references: Pober BR. Overview of epidemiology, genetics, and pathogenesis of congenital diaphragmatic hernia. UpToDate. 2023.
Orphanet: Non-syndromic diaphragmatic or abdominal wall malformation. ORPHA:108977.
Langham MR Jr, Kays DW, Ledbetter DJ. Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: epidemiology and outcome. Semin Pediatr Surg. 1996.
